title: Design a distributed key-value store
dek: Zotato keeps carts, sessions and app settings for 20 crore accounts: about a terabyte of small values, read lakhs of times a second. Build a store that spreads them over many machines, keeps three copies, and keeps working when a machine dies.

items: The API is tiny: get, put and delete by key. All the work is in where keys live and how copies agree.
Place keys with consistent hashing: machines and keys are hashed onto a ring, and each key lives on the next few machines clockwise. Adding a machine moves only a small slice of keys.
Keep three copies. A write waits for two to confirm, a read asks two; since 2 + 2 > 3, every read reaches at least one copy with the latest write.
Copies can disagree for a while. Version every value, return the newest, and repair stale copies in the background.
On each machine, writes go to a log on disk first, then to memory, and are written out in sorted files later. Fast writes, and nothing lost in a crash.
get(key), put(key, value), delete(key). Values are small, up to a few KB.
Keep working when a machine, or a whole zone, is down.
Grow by adding machines, without stopping or moving most of the data.
Out of scope here: queries by anything other than the key, and transactions across keys.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: Reads and writes in a few milliseconds
A confirmed write survives any one machine dying
Keeps answering with one zone of three down
20 crore accounts, about 1 TB, 2 lakh reads and 20,000 writes a second

items: Data: 20 crore accounts × about 5 KB of carts, sessions and settings is 1 TB. With three copies, 3 TB.
If each machine holds about 250 GB comfortably, that's 12 machines; run 15 to 20 so each has room to grow and to take a dead neighbour's share.
Reads: 2 lakh a second across 15 machines is about 13,000 each, fine for keys that are mostly in memory.
Writes: 20,000 a second, each sent to three copies, is 60,000 copy-writes a second across the cluster, about 4,000 per machine.
Value: `key`, `value` (bytes), `version` (rising, with the writer's id to break ties), `deleted` (a marker, so a delete isn't undone by an old copy).
Ring: which machines own which slices of the hash range, shared by every node and client library.

body.label: API
body.say: Read a key and its version. Write it, optionally only if it's still at the version you read. Delete it.

body.cap: Machines and keys are hashed onto a ring. cart:u_42 lands between A and B, so it's stored on the next three machines clockwise: B, C and D. When E joins, it takes over only the slice next to it.

body.x: Any machine can take a request: it works out the key's owners from the ring and talks to them. Clients can also do this themselves and go straight to an owner, saving a hop.

body.name: First try
body.kind: HASH MOD THE NUMBER OF MACHINES
body.use: Even spread, one line of code.
body.avoid: Go from 15 machines to 16 and almost every key's machine changes. Adding one machine means moving nearly the whole terabyte.
body.ex: Adding a machine before Diwali sends 94% of carts to new homes, while customers are shopping.
body.like: Renumbering every house in the street because one new house was built.

body.name: Better
body.what: Hash machines onto a ring of values, many times each (virtual nodes). A key belongs to the next points clockwise from its own hash.
body.use: Adding a machine moves only about 1/N of the keys, taken a little from every machine; losing one spreads its load over everyone.
body.avoid: Every node and client needs the same ring. Keep it in a small consensus-backed store (see the consensus article) and cache it.
body.ex: Going from 15 to 16 machines moves about 6% of keys, a little from each of the 15.
body.like: A new house gets a number between its neighbours; nobody else's address changes.

body.cap: A write waits for two of three copies; C was slow and missed it. A read asks two, B and C: B has version 8, so 8 is returned and C is repaired. With 2 + 2 > 3, every read overlaps the write.

items: N copies, W to confirm a write, R to answer a read. With N = 3, W = 2, R = 2, reads see the latest confirmed write.
Choose by need: carts use W = 2, R = 2; a "last seen" timestamp could use W = 1, R = 1 for speed, accepting a stale read now and then.
Put the three copies in three different zones, so losing a zone loses one copy, not two.
Two writers at once: give each value a version and write with "only if still version 8". The loser re-reads and tries again, instead of silently overwriting.
Machines tell each other who is up (gossip, or heartbeats to a coordinator). A machine that misses several is treated as down.
While a copy's owner is down, another machine takes its writes and hands them over when it's back.
Copies drift (a missed write, a disk error). A background job compares copies range by range, using hashes of each range so only differing ranges are sent, and fixes them.
A dead machine for good: its slices are copied from the surviving copies to new owners, from many machines at once.
A write is appended to a log on disk (so a crash loses nothing), then put in an in-memory table.
When the in-memory table fills, it's written out as a sorted file. Reads check memory, then the newest files first; a small filter per file skips files that can't have the key.
Files are merged in the background (compaction), dropping old versions and deleted keys after a while. This shape is called an LSM tree.
Junior / mid: get/put by key, partitioning across machines, copies for safety, a cache-like in-memory read path.
Senior: consistent hashing and virtual nodes, N/W/R and what they buy, versions and conditional writes, zones.
Lead: failure detection and handing writes over, repairing drift, adding and removing machines live, the LSM write and read path.
"One key gets very hot?" Cache it in front, or for counters split it into several keys and add them up (see the like counter in the photo-sharing question).
"Why not just use a database?" For this shape of data, a key-value store scales out more simply; a relational database is better when you need queries and transactions.
"Deletes come back to life?" That's why deletes are written as markers with a version and only cleaned up after every copy has seen them.
"Strong consistency for some keys?" Use a leader per slice chosen by consensus, and send those keys' reads and writes to it, at the cost of some speed.
"How do you test it?" Kill machines and cut network links during load, then check that every confirmed write can still be read, with the right version.

body.x: A confirmed write must survive a crash. The lost-orders challenge is about exactly that promise.
